items.q: Which statement about chromosomes and genes in a body cell is correct?
items.correct: Each chromosome carries a large number of genes.
items.misconception: A gene is made up of a large number of chromosomes.
items.why: Students meet the word gene first and in everyday language, so it feels like the 'big' idea, and the hierarchy of nucleus, chromosome, gene is easily reversed. The nucleus of a cell contains chromosomes made of DNA molecules, and each chromosome carries a large number of genes, so the chromosome is the larger structure.
items.random_wrong: Each chromosome carries one gene made of DNA.

items.q: How are the chromosomes normally arranged in a body cell?
items.correct: In pairs, held inside the nucleus of the cell.
items.misconception: Singly, inside the nucleus of the cell.
items.why: Diagrams of the cell cycle usually draw chromosomes singly and scattered, and students count the total number without noticing that they match up as pairs. In body cells the chromosomes are normally found in pairs.
items.random_wrong: In pairs, inside a large gene in the cell.

items.q: Which description gives the three overall stages of the cell cycle in the correct order?
items.correct: The cell grows and copies its DNA, the nucleus divides, then the cytoplasm divides.
items.misconception: The nucleus divides first, then the cell grows and copies its DNA, then the cytoplasm divides.
items.why: Mitosis is the stage that is drawn, animated and named most often, so the growth stage before it is treated as a gap rather than as a stage of the cell cycle. Before a cell can divide it needs to grow and increase the number of sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria. The DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome.
items.random_wrong: The cell grows and halves its DNA, then the nucleus divides, then the cytoplasm divides.

items.q: A human body cell containing 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis. What does each new cell contain?
items.correct: 46 chromosomes, identical to the parent cell
items.why: One cell becomes two, so students assume everything inside is shared out and halved, forgetting that the genetic material was doubled first. During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells, and in mitosis one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell.
items.random_wrong: 46 chromosomes, not identical to the parent cell

items.q: Before a cell divides it grows and increases its number of ribosomes and mitochondria. What happens to the DNA at this stage?
items.correct: The DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome.
items.misconception: The DNA is halved to leave one copy of each chromosome.
items.why: One cell becomes two, so students assume everything inside is shared out and halved, forgetting that the genetic material was doubled first. During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells, and in mitosis one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell.
items.random_wrong: The DNA replicates after the nucleus has divided in two.

items.q: What happens during mitosis and the stage that follows it?
items.correct: One set of chromosomes goes to each end, then the cytoplasm divides.
items.misconception: One set of chromosomes goes to each end, and the cell stays whole.
items.why: Mitosis is presented as the dramatic, well illustrated part of the cell cycle, so the final stage is easily left off the end of a description. Finally the cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells.
items.random_wrong: Half of each chromosome goes to each end, then the cytoplasm divides.

items.q: A cut on the arm of a fully grown adult heals as new skin cells are produced. Which statement about the new cells is correct?
items.correct: The new identical cells are produced by mitosis.
items.misconception: New cells with half the chromosomes are made.
items.why: One cell becomes two, so students assume everything inside is shared out and halved, forgetting that the genetic material was doubled first. During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells, and in mitosis one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell.
items.random_wrong: New genetically different cells are made.

items.q: Which statement describes a stem cell?
items.correct: An undifferentiated cell that can give rise to other cells.
items.misconception: A specialised cell that carries out one particular function.
items.why: Stem cells are taught alongside lists of specialised cells, so students file them as one more cell type with a function rather than as cells that have not yet differentiated. A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell of an organism which is capable of giving rise to many more cells of the same type, and from which certain other cells can arise from differentiation.
items.random_wrong: A bone marrow cell that forms most cell types in the body.

items.q: Which statement about the function of stem cells is correct?
items.correct: Meristem tissue can differentiate into any plant cell.
items.misconception: Bone marrow stem cells can differentiate into any type of cell.
items.why: Both sources are called stem cells, so students assume the two must be able to do the same job and ignore the difference in wording between the two statements. Stem cells from human embryos can be cloned and made to differentiate into most different types of human cells, while stem cells from adult bone marrow can form many types of cells including blood cells.
items.random_wrong: Embryonic stem cells are specialised for one particular job.

items.q: Which statement about therapeutic cloning is correct?
items.correct: An embryo with the same genes as the patient is produced.
items.misconception: The stem cells produced are rejected by the patient's body.
items.why: Students know that transplants are often rejected, and apply that rule to every cell or tissue that is put into a patient without checking whose genes the cells carry. In therapeutic cloning an embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient. Stem cells from the embryo are not rejected by the patient's body so they may be used for medical treatment.
items.random_wrong: The stem cells are taken from the patient's bone marrow.

items.q: Which statement about treatment with stem cells is correct?
items.correct: It may be able to help conditions such as paralysis.
items.misconception: It is a guaranteed cure for conditions such as paralysis.
items.why: News reports describe promising individual cases as breakthroughs, and the specification's careful wording 'may be able to help' is easily overstated in an answer. Treatment with stem cells may be able to help conditions such as diabetes and paralysis.
items.random_wrong: It uses bone marrow stem cells to replace nerve cells.

items.q: Which statement about the risks of using stem cells is correct?
items.correct: Viral infection could be transferred to the patient.
items.misconception: The concerns are ethical rather than medical ones.
items.why: Classroom discussion of stem cells concentrates on the debate about embryos, so the medical risk named in the specification is crowded out. The use of stem cells has potential risks such as transfer of viral infection, and some people have ethical or religious objections.
items.random_wrong: The cloned embryo's cells are rejected by the body.

items.q: Why are stem cells from meristems used to clone rare plant species?
items.correct: Identical plants are produced both quickly and economically.
items.misconception: Different plants are produced quickly and economically.
items.why: Students link cell division with the production of offspring, which they know vary, so they expect variation whenever cells divide. During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells.
items.random_wrong: Identical plants are produced slowly and at high cost.

items.q: How many genes does one chromosome carry?
items.misconception: Each chromosome carries just one gene, so a gene and a chromosome are really the same thing.
items.why: Textbook diagrams often label a single chromosome with one gene to keep the picture simple, and the two words are used in the same sentence so often that students treat them as interchangeable. The nucleus of a cell contains chromosomes made of DNA molecules, and each chromosome carries a large number of genes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does mitosis still happen in a fully grown adult?
items.correct: Yes, new identical cells are still produced by mitosis.
items.misconception: Mitosis stops once an organism has finished growing, so it happens in embryos and children but not in adults.
items.why: Mitosis is introduced as the process behind growth, so students tie it to a period of getting bigger rather than to the production of new identical cells. Cell division by mitosis is important in the growth and development of multicellular organisms and it continues in adults: for example, stem cells from adult bone marrow form many types of cells including blood cells.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When can meristem tissue produce new plant cells?
items.correct: Throughout the life of the plant.
items.misconception: Meristem tissue can produce new cells while a plant is young, and stops working once the plant is mature.
items.why: Students transfer what they know about animals, which reach a final adult size, onto plants, and assume plant growth must also stop. Meristem tissue in plants can differentiate into any type of plant cell, throughout the life of the plant.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How quickly and cheaply can plants be cloned from meristems?
items.misconception: Cloning plants from meristem stem cells is a slow and expensive process.
items.why: Students associate the word cloning with complicated animal cloning in laboratories, and do not connect it with the routine, cheap propagation of plants. Stem cells from meristems in plants can be used to produce clones of plants quickly and economically, so rare species can be cloned to protect them from extinction and crop plants with special features such as disease resistance can be cloned in large numbers for farmers.
